text: Good evening, mayor and council. I have with me tonight three of those mothers that you just saw who have lost children to the ravages of addiction. My name is Paul Hurgot and I'm speaking tonight on behalf of Citizens Helping Addicts and Alcoholics Get Treatment. Thousands of us who have come together in only a couple of months call ourselves CHAT, a grassroots group lobbying for a comprehensive strategy, a full-scale treatment facility to deal with Sault Ste. Marie's addiction crisis. As we have just seen, the stories are endless, the pain unending and the cost immeasurable. I don't believe there is anyone here this evening who has not been affected in some way by alcohol or drug addiction. People with addiction have a disease that requires medical treatment. We must remember that these are sick people who are doing bad things. They are not bad people doing bad things. Addiction must be treated as a medical disease, not a blight on our community. Therefore, like all people with a disease, they need medical treatment with dignity and respect. Those who use drugs and alcohol are not just those visibly marginalized and living in poverty. The majority of people suffering from addiction are not visible. They are working and living among us every day. The lack of facilities and care has brought us to a breaking point. Sault Ste. Marie has the highest opioid death rate in Ontario. Algoma Public Health estimated that 60 people would die in 2020 in Sault Ste. Marie from the opioid overdoses. Alcohol-related deaths also ravage our city. These are harder to track because the cause of death is usually attributed to liver or heart disease. Crime rates continue to rise. Impaired driving, property crimes, thefts, violent assaults, and murder. The local Crown has six murders and two attempted murders before the courts at this time. They are all drug-related. At least 102 firearms were seized in 2020. As well last year, close to $1 million worth of dangerous drugs were seized. Sault Ste. Marie Police Chief Hugh Stevenson tells chat that 80% of calls they receive are mental health and addiction related. The greater number being related to drugs. The police budget is around $30 million annually. Do the math. This is not just about death. It's about quality of life. Look around. You will see ravaged people, devastated families, and a community in despair. Discarded needles, plummeting property values, sex trafficking, family breakdown, job loss, organized crime, and gang activity. Add to that the cost of responding to the civic emergency. Police, ambulance, healthcare, the justice system. A continuum of care is desperately needed. Most communities in the North have a residential treatment center. We are the only community without a proper residential withdrawal management facility or a 28-day treatment center. Currently, we send our most vulnerable citizens elsewhere to access withdrawal and treatment. Places where they have no family or support network. Having to leave the community may prevent someone from reaching out for help. This is especially true for single parent homes. Figuring out aftercare is done on their own when they return from treatment. The wait for publicly funded treatment centers is currently three to four months. While the affluent can spend 20, 30, or $40,000 to get their loved ones into private facilities, others like Rhonda with us tonight are forced to sell their homes and belongings. The final insult is the cost of treatment is taxed. Until our full-scale treatment facility is operational, Sault Ste. Marie requires an adequate number of safe beds where people can stay while awaiting transfer to an out-of-town rehabilitation facility. CHAT's number one priority is to see our old detox, which closed in 2020, replaced with a new 20-bed residential medical withdrawal facility. The current makeshift detox at the Sioux area hospital is woefully inadequate and the screening process for admission goes against the whole philosophy of people self-admitting. In 2019, the Sault Ste. Marie and Area Drug Strategy Report was completed and released. It contained recommendations very similar to ours, yet nothing happened. Likewise, in 2010, the LHIN created a local group and funded them to the tune of $250,000 to look into the delivery of mental health and addiction services in Sault Ste. Marie. After one year, 187-page report, the LHIN suggested merging all mental health and addiction services. They found fragmentation of care, care being given in silos, and that the focus needed to be client care. The recommendations were never followed through on because of the cost implications for the LHIN and the refusal of some of the major healthcare providers to cooperate. The status quo is no longer acceptable. The time has come to stop doing studies that repeatedly produce the same recommendations. The time has come to implement a strategy that includes, but is not limited to, in-town treatment. We need a medical withdrawal clinic immediately and a 28-day rehabilitation facility. We need safe beds, a supervised consumption site, increased access to the RAM clinic, increased Canadian Mental Health Association accessibility. We need increased accessibility to the East Street Addiction Clinic. In closing, I ask, on behalf of everyone victimized by addiction in our community, how much was a life worth in 2020? How much will life be worth in 2021? All levels of government need to take action now. We need more money to support the existing clinics, caregivers, and programs that are currently operating. We need to expand our existing clinic hours and days of operation. We need to break the barriers for people getting help at the hospital emergency and be able to guide them into care. CHAT supports Council's Resolution 8.1, passed January 25th, requesting a residential treatment center for Sault Ste. Marie. I ask Mayor and City Council to show their support for what CHAT is requesting this evening so that we can move forward as a community with one goal and one purpose, to save lives. I would like to thank all the wonderful people who have joined CHAT, those devastated by addiction, yet brave enough to share their stories, those who have stepped up to support them. Thank you to everyone who is fighting for change. I would also, in closing, I would also like to thank specifically Robert Peace and Rolling Stone Pictures for their media and public relations support, without which we could not have got the community behind us. We also have many other people who we wish to thank, which are posted on the slide. And Mr. Mayor and Council, I look forward to hearing your support for these suggestions.
